title: Rarer stems, and one root across the stems

objectives.can: Recognise the rarer stems when met, and compare the forms and senses of one root in several stems.

explanation.summary: Besides the seven main stems, the Bible has a few rarer ones. Most are variants of the doubling stems, made for roots that cannot double in the usual way. Learning to recognise them completes the system. The best way to learn what stems do is to follow one root through several of them, verse by verse.

sections.heading: Polel, Poel and Hithpolel
body: Many roots have a vav or yod as their middle consonant, and these 'hollow' roots cannot double a middle consonant in the usual Piel way. They have a different doubling pattern: the Polel has a long o-vowel after the first root consonant and then repeats the last consonant: כּוֹנֵן, רוֹמְמוּ. It stands where the Piel stands for the strong verb, and is typically active. The Hithpolel is the Polel with the Hithpael's prefix, and it is typically reflexive: אֶתְבּוֹנֵן in 1 Kings 3:21 is 'I looked closely', and וְיִתְרוֹמֵם in Daniel 11:36 is 'he will exalt himself'. The Poel is a rarer variant of the Polel for roots whose second and third consonants are the same: the participle מְקֹשֵׁשׁ in Numbers 15:32 is 'gathering'.
The Polel is the commonest of these: the library's edition has about 180 Polel forms, about 110 Hithpolel and about 75 Poel.

sections.heading: Pilpel and Hishtaphel
body: The Pilpel repeats the first two root consonants of the pattern: וְכִלְכַּלְתִּי in Genesis 45:11, 'and I will sustain'. It is rare, and often marks repeated or intensive action or, in some verbs, a sound. The Hishtaphel is a stem with a prefix in -shtaph- that is found in practice in a single root, the verb 'bow down': וַתִּשְׁתַּחֲוֶיןָ in Genesis 37:7. Most modern grammars take the Hishtaphel as the right analysis of this verb; the older grammars analysed it as a Hithpael of a root with a different third consonant, with a sibilant exchanging place with the ת. Both views are held in the literature. The library's edition labels some forms Hithpael (וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ in Genesis 18:2) and others Hishtaphel, though they are the same verb in the same shape, so do not infer a difference of meaning from the label.

sections.heading: The Qal passive
body: A small number of forms look like Qal forms in the active and have a u-vowel for the passive: טֹרָף in Genesis 44:28, 'torn to pieces', beside the Qal infinitive absolute טָרֹף before it; and אֻכְּלוּ, 'they were eaten'. In the library's edition these are labelled Qal passive. The label is the edition's reading: other editions and grammars treat some of these forms as Pual or Hophal, and the Pual of one verse, לֻקֳחָה in Genesis 2:23, has the same look. Do not worry about the boundary. Recognise a passive by its u-vowel and its sense.

sections.heading: One root across the stems
body: The stems come to life when you follow one root. The root of רָם, 'high', shows how the system works. In the Qal it is stative: 'be high'. In the Hiphil it is causative: יָרִים in 1 Samuel 2:8, 'he lifts up'. In the Polel it is active: מְרוֹמֵם in 1 Samuel 2:7, 'he exalts'. The Hophal is the passive of the Hiphil: הוּרָם in Exodus 29:27. The Hithpolel is reflexive: וְיִתְרוֹמֵם in Daniel 11:36.

The root of כָּבַד has a different pattern. The Qal is 'be heavy': כָבְדָה in Genesis 18:20. The Niphal is 'be honoured': וְאִכָּבְדָה in Exodus 14:4. The Piel is 'honour': כַּבֵּד in Deuteronomy 5:16. The Hiphil is 'make heavy', and so 'harden': וַיַּכְבֵּד in Exodus 8:28. The Pual, יְכֻבָּד, is passive: 'is honoured'. These are tendencies of the stems at work on one root; each sense comes from the verse and from the lexicon, and a lexicon entry for a root is arranged by stem for this reason.

sections.heading: Using this in reading
body: When you meet an unfamiliar stem, do three things: name the pattern from the shape; ask which of the usual stems it stands in for (a Polel stands in for a Piel, a Hithpolel for a Hithpael); and look up the root in a lexicon, where the entry will list the stems found and their senses. Do not decide the sense from the stem alone.

misunderstandings: The rare stems are not rare forms of rare words. Some of the most common verbs, such as the verb 'bow down', are found in them.
The Polel is not a different sense from the Piel. It is the doubling pattern that hollow roots use, and it has the sort of meanings that a Piel has.
A root does not have every stem. A table of one root across the stems will have gaps, and the gaps are normal.
The same root in different stems does not give a regular set of senses. The Hiphil of one root is causative and of another is idiomatic.

deeper.heading: Hishtaphel or Hithpael?
body: The usual forms of the verb 'bow down' begin with -שתח-. The older analysis is that the root has a final he, that the form is a Hithpael, and that the ת has changed places with the sibilant; but this explanation does not account for all the forms. Most modern grammars therefore treat the forms as a Hishtaphel, a stem with a prefix of the shape -shtaph- that is known from related languages. The library's edition follows one analysis in some forms and the other in others; the course follows no one and names both.

examples.analysis: Three Hiphil participles and one Polel participle in a verse about what the LORD does. מוֹרִישׁ, וּמַעֲשִׁיר and מַשְׁפִּיל are Hiphil: 'makes poor', 'makes rich', 'brings low'. מְרוֹמֵם is a Polel participle, the Polel of the root of יָרִים in the next verse: 'exalts'. The doubled final consonant after a long o is the Polel pattern.
